$comment: The building that never has an off-peak, and the only shipped one whose worst case is a bed. A hospital's demand is two-way for eighteen hours a day and its peaks are SHIFT CHANGES rather than a morning arrival, which is why it ships with a `hospital` traffic profile and is meant to be run against the `shift-change` demand template rather than an office's rise-and-fall. Three things here exist nowhere else in data/buildings/. The bank holds FIVE UNLIKE CARS: three public cars at 3500 lb and 2.5 m/s beside two bed cars at 5000 lb, 1.6 m/s, side-opening, with a 3.0 s passenger transfer -- a trolley with an attendant and a drip stand is not a person stepping in, and CIBSE Guide D prices a bed transfer at roughly twice a passenger's. It is ONE bank because both kinds of car really do serve every floor; a second bank would make every floor a floor served by two banks, and `isTransferFloor` means sky lobby. It is the first shipped building to declare a `stairs` transport mode, so the asymmetric-propensity model of docs/14 SS 3.3 finally has a caller in data/ rather than only in a test fixture. And the entrance is not the only crowd source: Outpatients on floor 1 holds 180 people, so a clinic ending sends a burst DOWNWARD from an intermediate floor, which is a shape neither an office up-peak nor a residential down-peak produces.
name: St Jude Hospital

transportModes.name: Main stair, ground to outpatients
transportModes.$comment: CITED: the 4.0 m rise is this building's own floor-to-floor. Fruin's stair-flow work gives 0.15-0.20 m/s vertical climbing speed on a normal stair and roughly 1.35x that descending; at 0.155 m/s up and 0.21 m/s down a 4.0 m rise is 25.8 s and 19.0 s, rounded here to 26.0 and 19.0. DERIVED, not cited: the `use` pair. There is no published propensity for this building, so it is stated as an assumption rather than a measurement -- more people walk DOWN one floor than up, which is the asymmetry docs/14 SS 3.3 requires a stairs mode to express, and the magnitudes are chosen so the stair carries a visible but minority share. LIMITATION: a single flight between two adjacent floors is the only stair a low-rise hospital's occupants would reliably choose, so no ward-to-ward stair is declared; if one were, its measured hop count belongs beside it per data/buildings/README.md.

notes: One bank, five unlike cars. The two bed cars are the right car for a trolley and the wrong one for a visitor, and nothing in the config says so -- the dispatcher has only their speed, their capacity and their transfer time to go on. Whether it learns to leave them alone for ordinary hall calls is a measurable property, and no other shipped building can ask it.
Population 986 with only 70 of it below ground and NONE at the entrance. Unlike every office here, the entrance floor holds nobody: A&E arrivals are incoming traffic, not a resident population.

The clinical access zone covers theatres and critical care, and diagnostics covers the lower ground. Visitors hold neither credential, so a visitor calling from G can be carried to a ward and cannot be carried to a theatre -- access zoning does the work service zoning does elsewhere.
Floor-to-floor is 4.0 m throughout, deeper than an office, because hospital floors carry services and must clear a bed being wheeled under them.

The bed cars are 4000 lb, which is the largest capacity data/elevator-specs.json carries -- its table stops at 'Service / high-rise'. A real bed lift is larger, and the honest move was to take the reference data's ceiling rather than to invent a class for this building: the 3500 lb row is already labelled 'ADA stretcher', so a stretcher-capable car is inside the shipped data and a 2500 kg bed lift is not. If a bed-lift class is ever added it needs its own citation.

NAMED LIMITATION: the bed cars carry no per-car passengerTransferS. The hospital building-type default of 2.5 s applies to all five, and a bed car's authored 3.0 s was removed rather than kept, because the model has no notion of a bed as a UNIT: every derived bound that reads a car's transfer time multiplies it by the car's full person count, so a 26-person bed lift at 3.0 s produces an 84.5 s loading bound describing 26 people boarding one at a time -- a journey no bed lift makes. The heterogeneity that IS modelled is speed and capacity, which the engine reads honestly. Modelling a bed as an indivisible load is real work and is not done here.
